name: Dresden Brown
lede: Dresden Brown is a warm, yellowish brown first recorded by Robert Ridgway in 1912 and later catalogued again by Maerz and Paul, though why either source tied it to the German city of Dresden is undocumented in the sources we have.

sections.title: A city name, an unexplained choice
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 nomenclature places this hue on plate XV, hue 17 prime, tone k, and the ISCC-NBS system later classified it as a moderate yellowish brown, about 2.3 units from that block's reference color [1]. Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary lists the same color, dating its own first recording to 1912 as well, on plate 14 K 8 [1]. Neither source explains the tie to Dresden, long known for its porcelain and decorative arts, so whether the name points to a porcelain glaze, a textile dye, or simply the look of aged clay is undocumented here [1].

The nearest named colors on file are [[dirt-brown]] and [[dusty-hazel]], at The library also notes [[camel|Camel]] as a close relative in the same family of warm, muted browns [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a close match to this brown in 5,185 of 23,781 paintings, about 21.8 percent, and in 3,079 by the stricter within-painting measure, more common than 99 percent of the named colors we track [2]. Inside those paintings it most often reads as a light tone, 35 percent of the 3,079, rather than a shadow or accent [2]. It peaks in paintings from the 1300s, at 2.4 times the expected rate for that century's museum holdings [2]. Rosa Bonheur is its most devoted painter here, present in 10 of her 24 works in the archive, about 2 to 3 times the baseline for the museums those works come from [2].

The earliest match in our archive dates to the year 799, with the latest from 1959, 3,772 dated paintings in all, a floor rather than a true first appearance given how thin our earliest centuries are [2]. That is 1,113 years before the name's own earliest record in our sources, 1912: it describes a common, ordinary brown that long predates any Dresden association [1][2]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors, not pigment identifications[2].
